Chapter 7: Living with the Past—Memory, Denial, and the Struggle to Move On.
Over the years, even as life pressed forward, the past never really let go. If you walk across Rwanda’s rolling hills today, you’ll notice they’re dotted with memorials—simple stones, mass graves, and museums filled with photographs and names. Every year, on the anniversary of the genocide, the country comes to a gentle halt. Survivors come together, lighting candles, speaking the names of their loved ones, sharing tears and comfort.
For some, these rituals bring a sense of peace. Imagine a man who’s lost everyone he ever called family—he finds purpose in caring for a memorial garden, planting bright flowers where tragedy once unfolded. He greets visitors, sharing his story again and again. For him, remembering is a way to help protect the future, to make sure such horror isn’t repeated.
But not everyone feels ready to remember. In some communities, denial quietly takes hold. There are whispers—maybe the numbers weren’t so high, maybe the violence went both ways, or maybe it’s simply time to let go and move on. Some survivors find themselves alone with their grief, their pain brushed aside or left unspoken. Meanwhile, the government—wanting to keep the peace—cracks down on anything it sees as “divisionism.” But sometimes, that comes at the cost of open and honest conversations.
Picture a teacher at a rural school, trying to talk about the genocide with her class. Some kids are too young to remember. Others carry memories that are too painful to share. She walks a fine line, wanting to be truthful but also give them hope—offering the facts, but also inviting them to imagine a kinder future. It’s a delicate balance, and some days leave her feeling completely drained, but she knows it matters.
The fight over memory isn’t just about looking back—it shapes everything that comes next. How a society remembers its darkest moments can set the course for how it rebuilds. In Rwanda, remembering became both a heavy burden and a vital duty—a way to honor those lost, to warn those still here, and to lay down the first stones of a better tomorrow.
Still, the scars linger. Some survivors wrestle with nightmares and flashbacks, never quite able to shake that sense of being out of place. Others find ways to get by—through work, faith, or just by putting one foot in front of the other, day after day. Rwanda keeps moving forward, but the past is always close, like a shadow that never fully disappears.
